newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan launches new savings bond, demand brisk.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan launches new savings bond, demand brisk.

text.p: Kazakhstan launched its first National Savings Bonds (NSOs) on Wednesday to help cover its budget deficit and bank officials said demand was brisk as small investors sought a hedge against inflation.

Leyla Aliyeva, an official at Narodny Bank dealing with the issue, told Reuters that demand on the first day of the 10-day subscription period had exceeded expectations, but she could give no total estimate.
"The biggest investment so far has been 200,000 tenge," she said, adding that most people were putting in small amounts.

The finance ministry said the 12-month bonds would pay a coupon of 27.4 percent annual for the first quarterly tranche -- a rate set in line with the return on three-month T-bills at the September 10 auction.

The yield, equivalent to 6.85 percent per quarter, will be adjusted every three months and the finance ministry believes it will protect savings from inflation, which dropped to 0.7 percent in August from 1.8 percent in July.
The government has forecast 1996 inflation at no more than 26-28 percent.
Finance Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference last week that the main aims of the NSO issue were to help cover the budget deficit and protect people's savings.

This year's budget deficit is expected to be about 44 billion tenge, while the total NSO issue will be worth 1.3 billion tenge. The first tranche of the bonds, each with a nominal value of 1,000 tenge, was for 300 million tenge.
The issue was postponed several times to allow more time for a hard-sell advertising campaign.

"My husband and I decided to sign up for the bonds to protect our money in case something happens. The children will come and get it," said Raisa Fyodorovna, 71. "Let's hope they don't swindle us this time."

Some were more sceptical about state guarantees. "Nowadays nobody can guarantee anything and the state is the biggest swindler of all," said Taisiya Yegorovna, 60. "I personally buy dollars and put them aside."
The two banks acting as agents for the bond issue were Narodny Bank and Kazkommertsbank.
Narodny's Aliyeva said the NSOs offered better returns than bank accounts where deposits carry fixed interest rates of four to 25 percent annual.
The issue will remain open to individual Kazakh investors until September 20 after which any unsold bonds will be offered to institutional investors, including foreigners.
According to the finance ministry, banks will quote NSOs daily to allow holders to sell the paper on a secondary market.
Narodny Bank estimates that Kazakhstan's 17 million people hold about $1 billion in cash, with many preferring to keep their savings under the mattress rather than trust fledgling financial markets.

But the NSOs appear to have stirred some popular interest. "We have taken a bit from the pension and decided to invest," said 65-year-old Rumiya Kurimovna. "We're buying 10,000 tenge worth. Maybe we'll get back 15,000."
